To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the viewer needs to be able to relate to a character in order to find his or her discourse humorous; (2) a character’s discourse can be funny even if it does not contain any jokes or funny situations, and (3) a viewer’s cognitive effort is not always rewarded with laughter, which can lead to frustration and disappointment.

(a) the viewer’s cognitive interpretative path is the key to finding a dialogue or monlogue humorous, and that (b) the viewer’s interpretative paths are not only influenced by the character’s layer, but by other elements in the recipient’s layer as well.

the viewer’s perspective on sitcom discourse is a key element in the interpretation process, that the viewer’s cognitive interpretative paths are crucial in finding a dialogue or monological utterance humorous and that humour is not an end in itself, but rather a tool used by the writer to create a humorous effect.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the viewer’s cognitive interpretative paths contribute to the creation of humour in sitcom discourse, and how these interpretative paths can be described and explained.
the cognitive mechanisms that enable the audience to find a particular dialogue humorous and, consequently, relevant.
the question of what makes sitcom discourse relevant to viewers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the viewer’s cognitive interpretative path in the process of finding a dialogue or monologues humorous is a complex and multi-layered one.
the viewer’s perspective is the key to finding a dialogue humorous.
the humour in a sitcom is not only the product of the writer, but also the result of the interaction of the viewer’s cognitive system with the text.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
humour is a matter of relevance and that the viewer is the ultimate judge of whether or not a situation is humorous.
the viewer’s perspective is a necessary prerequisite for humour comprehension.
the viewer is the ultimate judge of what counts as humorous, and that humour is not an objective quality of discourse, but rather an individual and subjective one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
humour in situation comedy is not a mere matter of language, but of a complex cognitive process, which requires the viewer to make sense of the situation, the characters, and the discourse itself.
the viewer’s interpretation of humour in a sitcom episode is not a linear process.
the cognitive interpretative path is not a linear process, but rather a complex and multi-dimensional one.
